# Cardiac Amyloidosis: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Paradigms

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive and life-threatening infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1]. This deposition leads to wall thickening, myocardial stiffening, and a restrictive physiology. While once considered a rare and untreatable condition, recent advances in multi-modality imaging and targeted therapeutics have revolutionized the clinical approach and significantly improved patient prognosis [2, 3]. Over 95% of clinical cases are attributable to one of two amyloid precursor proteins: monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL amyloidosis) or transthyretin (ATTR amyloidosis) [4]. ATTR amyloidosis is further classified into a hereditary variant (ATTRv) caused by pathogenic mutations in the *TTR* gene, and a wild-type form (ATTRwt) associated with aging [5]. Correctly identifying the amyloid subtype is critical, as the treatment paths and prognoses for AL and ATTR differ completely [6].

AL amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency originating from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia that overproduces toxic free light chains [7]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis stems from the dissociation of the hepatic-derived homotetrameric transthyretin protein into unstable monomers, which subsequently misfold and self-assemble into amyloid fibrils [8]. ATTRwt is increasingly recognized as a major underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), particularly in elderly men [6, 8].

The clinical presentation of CA is predominantly characterized by progressive, treatment-resistant heart failure [9]. Classic diagnostic "red flags" include low-voltage complexes on electrocardiography (ECG) discrepant with severe left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiography, conduction system disease, carpal tunnel syndrome, and spinal stenosis [9]. Echocardiography typically serves as the first-line screening tool, characteristically demonstrating concentric ventricular hypertrophy, biatrial enlargement, and interatrial septal thickening [9]. Two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography demonstrates a highly specific pattern of "apical sparing," wherein longitudinal strain is preserved at the apex but severely reduced in the basal and mid-ventricular segments [10].

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides outstanding tissue characterization. Standard protocols demonstrate diffuse, subendocardial, or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) [11]. Furthermore, quantitative native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) calculations serve as sensitive markers for early-stage disease and provide a non-invasive quantification of myocardial amyloid burden [12].

A major paradigm shift occurred with the validation of non-biopsy diagnostic criteria for ATTR [13]. Bone-seeking radiotracers, such as $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-pyrophosphate (PYP) or $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (DPD), bind selectively to ATTR myocardial deposits [14, 15]. The presence of Perugini grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake, in the absolute absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, has a positive predictive value of virtually 100% for ATTR cardiomyopathy, obviating the need for endomyocardial biopsy [13, 16]. However, ruling out AL amyloidosis is a crucial first step. This requires serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and a serum free light-chain assay [13]. Any abnormality in these hematologic screens warrants urgent tissue biopsy and hematology consultation, as delayed treatment for AL amyloidosis carries a high risk of early mortality [17, 18, 19].

Prognostication in cardiac amyloidosis relies heavily on cardiac biomarkers. The Mayo Clinic staging systems utilize N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), cardiac troponins, and the difference in free light chains to stratify risk and guide therapeutic decisions [17, 18]. Systematic screening in high-risk HFpEF populations has proven essential for identifying subclinical disease [20]. Criteria for defining specific organ involvement and hematologic treatment response remain key to assessing clinical progress [21].

The management of cardiac amyloidosis is divided into supportive care and disease-modifying therapies [22]. Supportive management focuses on maintaining euvolemia with loop diuretics and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [22]. Traditional heart failure therapies, including beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers, are generally poorly tolerated and may exacerbate hypotension due to the restrictive ventricular physiology [22].

For AL amyloidosis, therapeutic strategies target the underlying clonal plasma cells. The current standard of care consists of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone, which has yielded remarkable hematologic and clinical responses [23]. Autologous stem-cell transplantation remains an option for eligible patients, and second-line agents are utilized for refractory disease [21, 24].

For ATTR amyloidosis, treatment has been revolutionized by targeted agents. Tafamidis, a small molecule that binds to the thyroxine-binding sites of the TTR tetramer, prevents dissociation and subsequent fibril formation. In a landmark clinical trial, tafamidis significantly reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations [25]. Tafamidis is also established in treating ATTR-associated polyneuropathy [26]. Additionally, gene-silencing therapeutics, including the small interfering RNA patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, inhibit hepatic TTR synthesis [27, 28]. Patisiran has been shown to improve cardiac structure and function, including reducing LV wall thickness and improving longitudinal strain [29, 30].

In conclusion, cardiac amyloidosis has transitioned from a historical terminal diagnosis to a highly manageable condition. Early diagnosis through multi-modality non-invasive imaging, combined with rapid subtype differentiation and the initiation of novel targeted disease-modifying therapies, has dramatically improved patient survival and quality of life.
